feature.imageCaption: The Universal Trail, Sunday, a little after sunset
feature.title: Twilight at Ijams strings the Universal Trail with lights and art on Sunday night, and it's the park's biggest fundraiser of the year
feature.deck: Small bites from local kitchens, a campfire with a s'mores bar, live music, a silent auction, and a trail of art installations between the Visitor Center and the woods, from six to nine. Tickets are $175, and the money is what keeps the park free the other 364 days.

body.text: Once a year Ijams Park dresses up. On Sunday evening the paved Universal Trail that runs from the Visitor Center into the trees gets strung with lights and lined with art installations, small plates come out of local kitchens, somebody starts a campfire with a proper s'mores bar beside it, and a band plays while the sun goes down over the ridge. It's called Twilight at Ijams, it is the park's largest fundraiser of the year, and this is the night.
What the ticket buys

A $175 ticket gets you in at six for three hours of food and drink — the bites are from local restaurants and caterers, and the bar runs beer, wine and cocktails. A $275 VIP ticket opens the doors an hour early for a cocktail hour at five. Tables of ten start at $1,500, which is how the park's bigger friends tend to show up. Along the way there's a silent auction and, the part that makes it more than a garden party, a run of what the park calls interactive vignettes and art installations set along the trail, so the walk itself is the show.
Why it costs what it costs

Ijams Park is free to walk every day of the year, and the nature center behind it is a nonprofit that runs on exactly this kind of night. Twilight is the one evening where the people who use the trails for nothing are asked, politely and with a drink in hand, to pay for them. If the ticket is out of reach, the park has other doors — memberships, the $15 walks and workshops that run every week — and the trail will look ordinary again by Monday morning.
If you're just out for a Sunday walk

Plan around it. Expect the Visitor Center end of the park — the lot, the lawn and the Universal Trail — to be a private event from late afternoon on. The Mead's Quarry side off Island Home Avenue, the Playscape and the trail network beyond it aren't part of the party, and the weekend's other Ijams Park events, the Friday fungi walk and Saturday's storytime, run as scheduled. Sunset Sunday is about a quarter to eight, so if you want to see the lights without a ticket, the river overlooks give you the ridge, not the trail.

stories.imageCaption: The part of the log you usually step over
stories.title: A beginner's mushroom walk opens Ijams Park's fall fungi series on Friday evening
stories.deck: Ninety minutes with an Ijams naturalist — what a mushroom actually is, how to tell it from a lichen, and how to look at a fallen log properly. Fifteen dollars, ages fourteen and up, and a week of storms should make the woods generous.

facts.label: When
facts.value: Fri Sep 11 · 5:30–7 PM

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Ijams Park · 2915 Island Home Ave

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: $15 · registration required

facts.label: Ages
facts.value: 14 and up

facts.label: The walk
facts.value: Up to 1.5 miles on uneven, rooty trail

facts.value: Water and closed-toe shoes · a signed risk form

facts.label: Next dates

body.text: Friday at half past five, an Ijams Park naturalist — the park's word is "fun-guide," and they know what they did — takes a small group out on the trails to look at the things growing on dead wood. It's the first walk of a four-part fall fungi series, and it's pitched squarely at people who have never done this: what a mushroom is, which parts are which, how to tell a fungus from a lichen, and how to start identifying what you find without eating anything to check.
What you'll actually see

That depends on the week, and this week has been good to mushrooms. After a run of ninety-degree days with afternoon storms, the low, shaded ground at Ijams Park is about as productive as it gets in September: shelf fungi on the logs, small capped mushrooms in the leaf litter, and the lichens that were there all along on the bark. The walk is a mile and a half at the most, on real trail with roots and rocks, and it stops a lot.
The practical part

Fifteen dollars, ages fourteen and up, and you need to register ahead — the page was still taking sign-ups Tuesday. Wear shoes you'd hike in, bring water, and expect a risk waiver at check-in. If Friday doesn't work, the same beginner walk repeats on September 20 and 27 and again October 18, when the fall crop is at its best.

body.text: A sports grill on a home-game Saturday is a waiting room: everybody's there until they aren't. The night it earns the televisions is the away game, and Tennessee's first one is Saturday at seven, at Georgia Tech in Atlanta, on ESPN. Puckers — the Gatlinburg sports bar that took the old Mimosas room on Mimosa Avenue two weeks ago — gets its first real test of the wall.
The game itself

Tennessee hasn't played at Bobby Dodd Stadium since 1986, and Georgia Tech is the kind of September opponent that turns a comfortable evening into a long one if the Vols start slow. It's a night kickoff, so it's a full evening: sit down at six, and the fourth quarter lands around half past ten.
The practical part

Puckers takes reservations on Resy, and for a seven o'clock kickoff a booked table beats a hopeful one. Its weekday Pucker Hour — the dollar lager, the three-dollar wells — runs Monday through Friday from five to six and does not extend to Saturday, so don't plan the budget around it. Last Saturday the room opened at nine in the morning and ran until ten at night; this week's hours weren't posted as of Tuesday. If the wall is full, Hi-Wire's rooftop and the SouthSide Garage beer garden on Sevier Avenue both keep the game on.

body.text: Friday night One Knox turns its home ground into a beer festival with a soccer match attached. It's KnoxtoberFest: gates and the biergarten open at five, a live polka band plays under the string lights, the first thousand fans over twenty-one get a beer stein to keep, and beer is three dollars all match long. Kickoff against FC Naples is at 7:06.
The soccer part

One Knox won USL League One last year, and this season's team is sitting on eleven wins, five losses and seven draws — four of those draws in a row coming into Friday, which is the polite way of saying they've forgotten how to close. Naples is a first-year club from Florida. On a theme night the match is the second-best reason to go, and the club knows it.
From this side of the river

Covenant Health Park is in the Old City, which is over the water from us — but only just. From the Sevier Avenue end of the neighborhood it's the Gay Street bridge and a few blocks, a mile or so on foot and five minutes in a car, and the walk back over the bridge with a stein in your bag is half the point. Three-dollar beer is a promotion, not an invitation to drive home on it.

stories.deck: Free, ten to noon, under the trees at Mead's Quarry. A story read out loud, then a nature craft or free play in the Playscape, every Saturday from now into the new year.

body.text: Storytime at the Nature Playscape has been a summer habit; Saturday it becomes a season. The fall run starts September 12 and goes sixteen Saturdays, ten to noon, at the Playscape by Mead's Quarry — the log-and-rope play area on the Island Home Avenue side of Ijams Park where the trees do the shade.
How a morning runs

Somebody reads a nature story out loud to whoever's on the blankets. Then, on alternating weeks, the group either does a hands-on activity that goes with the book — a leaf craft, a bug hunt, that sort of thing — or simply turns the kids loose on the Playscape with an adult keeping a loose eye. It's two hours on the schedule; most families do one and drift.
The fine print

It's free, and it will stay free through the whole run. The one cost is the Mead's Quarry lot, which is five dollars a car unless you're an Ijams member. Bring your own seat, your own water and a snack — there's no concession on that side of the park — and note that Sunday's fundraiser doesn't touch this end of Ijams at all.

body.text: Earl's, down at the water on Waterfront Drive, keeps a different deal for every day of the weekend, and the ladder hasn't moved: ten-dollar Patrón mango margaritas during Thursday's happy hour, nine-dollar spicy pineapple ones Friday, eight-dollar house margaritas from open to close Saturday, and seven-dollar mimosas and Bloody Marys all day Sunday. Thursday and Friday the happy hour is four to six, and a dollar comes off liquor, beer and wine for the rest of the night.
One honest note

This board was last confirmed against Earl's own specials page on September 1. The page wouldn't load for us Tuesday, so if a price has moved, the chalk on the patio wins. The river seats go first regardless — get to Suttree Landing by turning toward the water at the Citgo on Sevier Avenue and following Claude Street down.
